attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: The revised proposition keeps both hedges, 'for the most part' and 'it appears', and frames the first half as his own search result.

contract.note: Fair. The first half reports his own search, which can't be checked. The 18-month figure is an explicitly hedged impression with no defined population or end point, so imposing a benchmark would be wrong.

evidence.note: Epoch's Abilene row shows about 16 months from land clearing to operation. It is one large site, not his sample, and the claim is hedged, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: Both halves fail to give a scorable claim. The first reports his own unverifiable search. The second is hedged ('for the most part, it appears') and has no defined measure. Under policy, hedged impressions are not scored.

attribution.note: His own assertion, made in reply to Microsoft's quoted wording.

semantics.note: His 'it didn't' answers the single quoted 'added another gigawatt' (the latest quarter). The drafter's 'each of its last two quarters' widens the claim. The contract correctly narrows it to Jan-Mar 2026.

contract.note: Reading 'brought online' as energized, usable capacity (owned or leased) is the ordinary reading of his words, and his firm 'obviously hasn't' allows a plain reading. Limiting the test to Jan-Mar 2026 fits the statement.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own 'added another gigawatt' wording. It is a company disclosure and doesn't define energized or live, so it can't settle the dispute.
The prior quarter's 'nearly 1 GW', which is the referent of 'another'. Same undefined term, and outside the target period.
A count of datacenters added in the fiscal year, with no megawatts, timing or energization status for Jan-Mar 2026.
Epoch shows one non-Fairwater site adding about 28 MW in the quarter. It covers part of the footprint and none of the leased capacity, so it can't confirm or refute about 1 GW.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet measures Microsoft's energized capacity added in Jan-Mar 2026. Microsoft's statements use the disputed term without defining it, and Epoch covers only part of the owned footprint and none of the leased capacity. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: His own summary in his own post.

semantics.note: The revised proposition keeps 'across the board' and the 'seems' hedge, and states the size-delay pattern as he gave it.

contract.note: Fair. 'The message seems to be' marks this as a hedged impression from his own survey. 'Build' and the size effect are undefined, so a plain reading should not be imposed.

evidence.note: Epoch reports 1-3.6 years to reach 1 GW at the largest sites. This concerns gigawatt campuses and a different milestone, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The generalization is hedged ('seems'). It gives no measure of build time (first phase or full campus) and no defined size bands or schedule baseline, so there is no fair test.

attribution.note: His own assertion, backed in context by 'If I was wrong...'.

semantics.note: 'I think in reality... if that' reads as a firm belief about a figure, not a graded probability. The proposition keeps the ceiling, 'usable', and 'each quarter'.

contract.note: Fair, ordinary reading: about 500 MW or less, worldwide, operational capacity, tested on the latest full quarter before the post. Relying on independent measurement respects his distrust of company claims.

evidence.note: New Carlisle went from not operational (Feb 9) to operational (Mar 23), adding about 284 MW of IT power, firmly inside Q1 2026.
Prometheus added about 292 MW, dated Jan 18 2026. The prior row is October, so some timing uncertainty.
Nusajaya added about 190 MW, dated Jan 2026 and backed by DayOne's in-service report. The prior row is Dec 2024, so the timing is weaker.
Epoch's error bands: capacity within 1.4x and dates within 6 months, 80% of the time. Adds uncertainty but doesn't reverse the result.

reviews.rationale: Epoch's site-level estimates put about 766 MW of IT power coming online in Q1 2026 at just three sites. e1 and e2 alone come to about 576 MW, and coverage is partial. That clearly exceeds 'a few hundred, if that'. Error bands and timing uncertainty weaken the margin but don't remove it.
